title: Draft Answer with Affirmative Defenses to Breach of Contract Complaint

blind.coverage: I read all 12 supplied documents in full: the complaint, MSA, PO-147, PO-163, Tranche 1 rejection email chain, Ted Caldwell settlement email, force majeure notice, termination notice, Meridian FM rejection letter, Nov. 18 letter and Jan. 8 demand letter, Tidewater suspension notice, and the Tranche 2 bill of lading. I also read task.json (all 40 criteria), the judge prompt (which shows the judge the criterion title as well as the match_criteria), and the start of the solver system prompt. I used grep across all documents to check facts that criteria rely on: the $180,000 retooling cost, resale, Irongate/Bartow County, and the interest basis. I recomputed dates: Sept 27, 2024 is the 11th business day after the Sept 12 delivery, the 15th is Oct 3, and Oct 2 to Oct 9 is 5 business days. On CourtListener I confirmed the Georgia rule that an express contract bars unjust enrichment. I found it quoted in Shlapak v. Dau (Ga. Ct. App. 2025), which quotes Marvin Hewatt Enters. v. Butler Capital. A search for a Georgia 'Benton v. Benton' unjust-enrichment case returned nothing. I did not read the statute text of O.C.G.A. 11-2-706, 11-2-709, or 13-6-5. Two things I noticed but did not flag, because neither changes a correct answer: (1) the two POs give different jobsite addresses (4500 Savannah River Industrial Parkway vs. 4500 River Reclamation Way); (2) Caldwell's FM and termination notices are addressed to 'Contracts Administration', not the 'Vice President of Sales' named in MSA 19.1.

findings.title: C-010 requires a $180,000 retooling cost and a 'modification for other buyers' fact that no document contains
findings.explanation: To PASS, the failure-to-mitigate defense must reference Meridian's non-resale 'despite the possibility of modification for other buyers (at approximately $180,000 retooling cost)'. A search of all 12 documents finds no retooling cost, no $180,000 figure, and nothing saying the custom valves could be modified for other buyers. The only record support for non-resale is Ted Caldwell's email ('should have been looking for other buyers') and Complaint para. 51 (units 'remain in storage'). A solver cannot meet the PASS text without inventing a fact. A strict judge may fail a correct, record-faithful defense. A lenient judge relies only on the FAIL clause ('not asserted'). So the outcome depends on which judge reads it, not on the quality of the answer.

evidence.quote: despite the possibility of modification for other buyers (at approximately $180,000 retooling cost)
Frankly, Meridian should have been looking for other buyers for the remaining inventory rather than sitting on it and running up a claim against us.
the units were returned to Meridian's Savannah warehouse, where they remain in storage.

findings.suggested_fix: Delete the retooling parenthetical. Require only that the defense assert Meridian failed to make reasonable efforts to resell or redeploy the Tranche 2, Tranche 3 and PO-163 inventory.

findings.title: C-017's 'correct' interest figure ($78,720 from Nov 1, 2024) has no record basis and ignores MSA 7.4
findings.explanation: The PASS test itself (deny or challenge $148,927.80 as incorrect) is sound. The embedded benchmark is wrong on the record. The demand letter gives Meridian's actual method: interest on the full $4,730,400 from October 9, 2024 through January 8, 2025. Yet the Complaint claims the same figure 'as of the date of this Complaint' (March 5). Nothing in the record supports a November 1, 2024 due date. On Meridian's own deemed-acceptance theory, acceptance falls on Oct 3 (15th business day) and payment is due about Nov 17 (45 days later), so the '4.1 months / $78,720' math does not follow. MSA 7.4 also stops interest on good-faith-disputed amounts. MSA 7.3 has no compounding, although Complaint para. 17 alleges it. A judge anchored on the $78,720 figure may undervalue a correct answer that argues zero interest or a different computation, and a bare 'Denied' sits uneasily with 'identifying it as ... miscalculated'.

evidence.quote: interest accrues on such accelerated amounts from the date of Caldwell's repudiation, October 9, 2024. Interest continues to accrue on the outstanding principal balance of $4,730,400.00 at the per diem rate of $2,363.40
($1,280,000 at 1.5% per month for approximately 4.1 months from November 1, 2024 to March 5, 2025) would be approximately $78,720
The disputed amount shall not accrue interest under Section 7.3 during the pendency of the dispute

findings.suggested_fix: Remove the specific 'correct' calculation. Instead, pass any answer that denies the figure or challenges its basis: acceleration on undelivered or unaccepted goods, the demand-letter/Complaint date mismatch, compounding not in 7.3, the 7.4 dispute tolling, or that no amount was due.

findings.title: C-007 recognizes only 'waiver', leaving a gap for other valid theories that answer the email-notice problem
findings.explanation: MSA 18.4 says no waiver is effective unless it is in writing and signed by the waiving party. That makes a conduct-based waiver argument contestable, though pleadable. A competent answer may instead argue that: 6.1 requires only 'written notice' and the email was written and actually received; the notice's purpose was served (actual notice / substantial compliance); or Meridian is estopped because Densmore responded substantively the same day. Such an answer neither admits the rejection was defective (the FAIL condition) nor asserts 'waiver' (the PASS condition). It falls between the two, and a judge would likely fail it for not meeting PASS.

evidence.quote: PASS if the Answer argues or asserts that Meridian waived the formal notice requirement ... FAIL if the Answer admits the rejection was defective without asserting waiver.
No waiver of any provision of this Agreement shall be effective unless made in writing and signed by the waiving Party.

findings.suggested_fix: Pass waiver, estoppel, actual notice/substantial compliance, or a textual 6.1 argument that email satisfies the 'written notice' requirement. FAIL only if the Answer concedes the rejection was ineffective.

findings.title: C-005 leaves 40-49 responses undefined, its title contradicts its threshold, and it omits Rule 8(b)(5) responses
findings.explanation: PASS needs 50 or more individually numbered responses and FAIL needs fewer than 40, so an answer with 40-49 has no defined outcome. The title says 'every numbered paragraph' (the Complaint has 91), the text says 50, and the judge prompt shows both. The allowed response forms (Admit, Deny, Admit in part) leave out 'lacks knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief' under Rule 8(b)(5). A correct answer will use that response for paragraphs about Meridian's internal facts (e.g., paras. 2, 29, 47). A literal judge might not count those paragraphs.

evidence.quote: PASS if the Answer contains individually numbered paragraph-by-paragraph responses (Admit, Deny, or Admit in part and deny in part) to at least 50 numbered paragraphs ... or responds to fewer than 40 individually numbered paragraphs.

findings.suggested_fix: Use a single threshold, or require responses to all 91 paragraphs (grouped responses allowed). Expressly count Rule 8(b)(5) lack-of-knowledge responses as valid.

findings.title: C-029 relies on a 'Bartow County Petrochemical Facility' fact that appears nowhere in the record
findings.explanation: The only mention of Irongate is Complaint para. 6. No document says the Irongate purchase was for a Bartow County project or had different specifications. The PASS test can be met with a plain denial of para. 6's characterization, so the risk of misgrading is low. But the rubric states facts as true that the solver cannot know. A judge primed with them might fault an answer that says, accurately, that Caldwell lacks the record to explain the Irongate transaction.

evidence.quote: The Irongate purchase was for a completely different project (Bartow County Petrochemical Facility) with different specifications.
Upon information and belief, Caldwell has separately retained industrial valve components from an alternative supplier, Irongate Fabrication Co.

findings.suggested_fix: Delete the Bartow County rationale. Keep only the test: the Answer must not admit or suggest that the Irongate goods replaced Meridian's goods for the Project.

findings.title: C-035's title names 'Caldwell's prior material breach' when the body means Meridian's breach
findings.explanation: The judge prompt shows the criterion title. The title says 'Caldwell's prior material breach / breach by plaintiff', but the match_criteria requires a defense based on Meridian's breach (defective Tranche 1 goods, wrong-location Tranche 2 delivery). The body is explicit, so the risk is low, but the mismatched title could confuse a judge.

evidence.quote: Affirmative defense: Caldwell's prior material breach / breach by plaintiff
PASS if the Answer asserts as an affirmative defense that Meridian itself breached the MSA

findings.suggested_fix: Retitle to 'Affirmative defense: Meridian's prior material breach / breach by plaintiff'.

findings.title: C-025 demands a separate 'Reservations' section, which is customary but not a required part of an answer
findings.explanation: A reservation of the right to amend or add defenses has no legal effect: amendment is governed by Rule 15 regardless. Many competent answers end the defenses with a one-sentence reservation rather than a separate section, and some omit it. The '(or substantially equivalent section)' hedge helps. Still, a judge applying 'separate ... section' literally could fail an answer that reserves rights in a closing sentence.

evidence.quote: PASS if the Answer includes a separate 'Reservations' section (or substantially equivalent section) that expressly preserves Caldwell's right to amend

findings.suggested_fix: Pass any express reservation of the right to amend or add defenses or counterclaims, wherever it appears.

findings.title: C-026 requires the words 'with prejudice' in the prayer; many competent prayers use 'take nothing' language
findings.explanation: Asking for dismissal with prejudice is common. An equally standard prayer asks for judgment for Defendant and that Plaintiff take nothing, which has the same effect. Read literally, C-026 would fail that answer. The risk is low but real under the all-pass metric.

evidence.quote: FAIL if no prayer for relief is included or if it does not request dismissal with prejudice.

findings.suggested_fix: Also pass a prayer that asks for judgment in Caldwell's favor and that Plaintiff take nothing, or equivalent final-disposition language.

findings.title: C-011 calls O.C.G.A. 11-2-706 / UCC 2-708 a 'seller's duty to resell'; under the UCC, resale is an optional remedy
findings.explanation: Under Georgia's UCC, resale under 11-2-706 is an optional remedy for the seller, not a duty. The mitigation-like limit is in 11-2-709(1)(b): the seller can sue for the price of unaccepted goods only if it cannot resell them after reasonable effort. Georgia's general duty to lessen damages is O.C.G.A. 13-6-5. The criterion also accepts 'general mitigation principles', so it should not misgrade a competent answer. But it frames the law imprecisely and implies a citation requirement for a short-form affirmative defense.

evidence.quote: references the seller's duty to make reasonable efforts to resell goods, whether citing Georgia's UCC provisions (O.C.G.A. § 11-2-706 or UCC § 2-708)

authorities.proposition: A seller can recover the price of goods not accepted only if it cannot resell them at a reasonable price after reasonable effort
Georgia's general duty of an injured party to lessen damages

findings.suggested_fix: Rephrase to cite 11-2-709(1)(b), 11-2-706 as an available remedy, 13-6-5, or general mitigation principles, and do not call resale a duty under 2-706.

findings.title: C-016's example authority 'Benton v. Benton' could not be found; the underlying Georgia rule is correct
findings.explanation: The Georgia rule is correct: where an express contract exists, there can be no recovery on unjust enrichment. I confirmed it in Shlapak v. Dau, which quotes Marvin Hewatt Enters. v. Butler Capital. A CourtListener search of Georgia appellate courts found no 'Benton v. Benton' decision on unjust enrichment. The example is offered as 'such as ... or similar', so it does not decide grading. But it could lead a judge to treat an unverifiable citation as good authority. C-016 also largely duplicates C-015.

evidence.quote: Georgia case law (such as Benton v. Benton or similar)

authorities.citation: Shlapak v. Dau (Ga. Ct. App. June 18, 2025), quoting Marvin Hewatt Enters., Inc. v. Butler Capital Corp., 761 S.E.2d 857 (Ga. Ct. App. 2014)
authorities.proposition: Where there is an express contract, there can be no recovery based upon an unjust enrichment theory

findings.suggested_fix: Replace the example with a verified Georgia authority (e.g., Marvin Hewatt Enters. v. Butler Capital) or drop the case-name example.

blind.overall: The rubric is mostly sound and closely tied to the record. The caption, count-denial, 13.2 termination-for-convenience, wrong-location Tranche 2 delivery, AQL/whole-shipment rejection, $960,000 arithmetic error, timeliness, and section-number criteria all check out against the MSA, the POs and the correspondence. The main defect is C-010: its PASS clause requires a $180,000 retooling fact that appears in no document, so it could fail a correct answer depending on the judge. C-017 and C-029 also contain explanatory 'facts' with no record basis, but their pass tests are lenient enough that misgrading is less likely. The remaining findings are ambiguity or phrasing problems that could fail some competent answers under the all-pass metric: C-007 (waiver-only), C-005 (the 40-49 gap), C-025 and C-026 (form requirements), and C-035's mismatched title. None of the core legal propositions the rubric rewards is wrong for Georgia law, though C-011 frames UCC resale imprecisely and C-016 cites an example case I could not find.

sol_verdicts.reason: The Complaint has 91 numbered paragraphs, and the title says 'every numbered paragraph'. PASS, however, needs only 50, and FAIL applies below 40, so 40-49 has no defined result. Under Rule 8(b)(6), an allegation left unanswered is admitted, so an answer that skips 41 paragraphs is materially deficient but still passes. The listed response forms also leave out Rule 8(b)(5) lack-of-knowledge responses. I have moved this up from my blind 'arguable'.

MSA 13.2 also requires reimbursement of documented, non-cancellable raw-material costs, capped at the PO value. The FM rejection letter says Meridian had begun buying raw materials for Tranche 3 and PO-163, so the omission matters. Still, an accurate answer that pleads the manufactured-goods limit plus raw materials would satisfy the PASS text. Caldwell's own termination notice also frames the obligation as goods only. The criterion is incomplete, but misgrading is unlikely, so arguable rather than confirmed.

Under MSA 7.1, payment is due 45 days after acceptance or deemed acceptance, and 7.4 stops interest on good-faith disputed amounts. Nothing supports a November 1, 2024 due date. The $78,720 'correct' figure also assumes the full $1,280,000 for Tranche 1 was owed, which contradicts the rubric's own C-033/C-037 position that the rejection was timely. The PASS test itself (deny or challenge the figure) is sound. The embedded 'correct' calculation states wrong facts.

Caldwell gave a timely FM notice (Oct 9, five business days after the Oct 2 suspension), and its termination notice expressly preserves the FM position. Section 12.1's list of events is non-exhaustive and includes 'government action'. Pleading FM in an answer is standard, low-cost practice that a competent practitioner would follow. C-009 expressly allows for the classification weakness and passes any answer that also pleads alternative defenses. Neither criterion misgrades competent work.

UCC 2-706 makes resale optional: the seller 'may resell'. The resale-effort limit is in 2-709(1)(b), which conditions an action for the price of unaccepted goods. Calling this a 'duty to resell' under 2-706/2-708 is imprecise. The criterion also accepts 'general mitigation principles', so competent answers should pass. This matches my blind finding.

Rule 15 governs amendment, so a reservation of rights has no legal effect. It is common boilerplate, but it is not a required part of an answer. The 'separate ... section' wording could fail a competent answer that reserves rights in one sentence or leaves the reservation out. The 'substantially equivalent' hedge lowers but does not remove that risk.

I confirmed this. Complaint paras. 1 and 7 place Meridian's principal place of business in Savannah, Georgia, and allege that all of Caldwell's members are Georgia citizens. Under 28 U.S.C. 1332(c)(1), a corporation is a citizen of its principal-place-of-business state, so complete diversity is absent. A competent answer would deny paras. 7-8 and ask for dismissal for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, which is without prejudice. Answers that pray for 'take nothing' judgment would also risk failing.

This is a note about Sol's own verification gaps, not a separate defect. The C-011 issue is covered by arguable/1. I read the model UCC 2-706(1) and 2-709(1) text, which supports treating resale as optional, with resale effort conditioning a price action under 2-709(1)(b).

findings.title: C-026 mandates 'with prejudice' although the record shows no complete diversity, and it fails 'take nothing' prayers
findings.explanation: Complaint para. 1 places Meridian's principal place of business in Savannah, Georgia. Para. 7 alleges that all of Caldwell's members are Georgia citizens. Under 28 U.S.C. 1332(c)(1), Meridian is therefore a Georgia citizen too, so complete diversity is lacking; para. 8 relies on incorporation alone. The rubric does not address this record issue. A competent answer would deny paras. 7-8, plead lack of subject-matter jurisdiction (which cannot be waived under Rule 12(h)(3)), and pray for dismissal, which is without prejudice. An answer that prays only for jurisdictional dismissal fails C-026. So does an equally standard prayer for judgment that Plaintiff take nothing. An answer that adds a with-prejudice prayer in the alternative passes, so this is arguable rather than certain.

evidence.quote: with its principal place of business at 2200 Commerce Park Drive, Suite 400, Savannah, Georgia 31405

FAIL if no prayer for relief is included or if it does not request dismissal with prejudice.

authorities.proposition: A corporation is a citizen of every state where it is incorporated and of the state where it has its principal place of business

findings.suggested_fix: Pass any prayer seeking final disposition in Caldwell's favor: dismissal with prejudice, take-nothing judgment, or jurisdictional dismissal with merits relief in the alternative. Consider adding credit for identifying the diversity defect.

findings.title: C-014 states MSA 13.2 incompletely, omitting the raw-material reimbursement obligation and the PO-value cap
findings.explanation: Section 13.2 also requires the terminating party to reimburse reasonable, documented, non-cancellable raw-material costs, subject to mitigation, with the total capped at the PO's value. The record makes this relevant: Meridian's FM rejection letter says it had begun buying raw materials for Tranche 3 and PO-163. C-014 rewards describing liability as 'limited to' manufactured or in-process goods, which misstates the contract. The risk of misgrading is modest. An accurate answer still pleads the goods limit and should pass, and Caldwell's own termination notice frames the obligation as goods only.

evidence.quote: The terminating Party shall also reimburse the non-terminating Party for reasonable, documented, non-cancellable costs of raw materials procured specifically for the terminated Purchase Order
Meridian has also begun procurement of raw materials for Tranche 3 of PO-147 and for PO-163
Caldwell's obligation upon termination for convenience is limited to paying for conforming goods already manufactured or in the process of manufacture

findings.suggested_fix: Describe the 13.2 exposure as manufactured and in-process conforming goods plus qualifying raw-material costs, capped at PO value. Expressly pass an answer that states either the full formula or the goods limit.

final.changes_from_blind: (1) I raised C-005 from arguable to problematic. I accept Sol's point that PASS at 50 of 91 paragraphs rewards an answer that is materially deficient under Rule 8(b)(6), on top of the 40-49 gap and the mismatch between title and threshold. (2) I raised C-017 from arguable to problematic. On re-checking, the 'correct' $78,720 figure contradicts MSA 7.1 and 7.4, and it also contradicts the rubric's own Tranche 1 position (C-033, C-037, C-020): it assumes the full $1.28M was owed from Nov 1. (3) I expanded my C-026 finding with Sol's jurisdiction point, which I verified. Meridian's principal place of business is in Georgia (Complaint para. 1), and all of Caldwell's members are alleged Georgia citizens, so under 28 U.S.C. 1332(c)(1) there is no complete diversity. A competent answer would seek dismissal without prejudice, which C-026's 'with prejudice' requirement would fail unless the prayer adds merits relief in the alternative. I kept it arguable. (4) I adopted C-014 as arguable, not confirmed. MSA 13.2 also requires raw-material reimbursement, and the FM rejection letter shows Meridian had begun raw-material procurement, but an accurate answer would still pass. (5) I reject Sol's C-008/C-009 finding as not a defect: pleading FM is standard, and C-009 already accounts for its weakness. (6) I verified the model UCC 2-706(1) and 2-709(1) text for C-011. All other blind findings are kept and renumbered.
final.overall: The rubric is mostly tied to the record.
